prime.problem: A plain lock answers "is anyone inside?" but not "who?". Without an owner, a method that calls another locked method waits on itself forever, and a stray release from the wrong thread lets two threads in. And when the lock is taken, the waiter must either burn a core spinning or pay a sleep and a wake-up.
prime.fits: Second Synchronization card. It refines the lock from the last card with ownership, reentrancy and a choice of how to wait; semaphores (next) drop ownership on purpose.
expect: 58 ns uncontended vs a 4.1 µs hand-off
prime.goal: Say when a plain mutex, an RLock or a spinlock fits, predict a self-deadlock from code, and explain why contention costs far more than the lock itself.

attend: What two fields does an RLock keep that a plain Lock doesn't, and how do they let withdraw() re-enter?
Why did another thread's release() succeed on a Lock but raise on an RLock?
When is spinning cheaper than sleeping, and what goes wrong with spinning on one CPU when the holder is descheduled?
Where does the 71× gap between 58 ns and 4.1 µs come from, and why does it make a hot lock line waiters up?
Why does the card prefer a plain mutex over RLock everywhere, even though RLock never self-deadlocks?

must: A plain Lock records no owner → the same thread re-acquiring it waits on itself → self-deadlock (acquire(timeout=0.1) → False) → RLock records owner + count → the owner re-enters (count 1 → 2 → 1 → 0)

Ownership = only the locker may unlock → a stray release from another thread is an error, not a silent second entry → that check is what separates a mutex from a binary semaphore → Python's plain Lock doesn't enforce it; RLock does

Free lock → one atomic instruction, no syscall (58 ns) → taken lock → sleep in the kernel and be woken (≈ 4.1 µs hand-off) → contention costs ~71× the lock → hot locks form convoys moving at one wake-up per step → hold them less (shorter sections, sharding)

Spin vs sleep depends on who holds the lock → holder running on another core and releasing soon → spinning wins → holder descheduled → spinners waste whole slices → two-phase locks spin briefly, then sleep
elevated: with lock: costs 87 ns vs 58 ns bare → 29 ns of with-statement overhead → irrelevant next to a 4.1 µs contended hand-off, so always use with for safety
reference: the exact RuntimeError text for releasing an un-acquired RLock

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the four-step transfer/withdraw trace for a Lock and for an RLock side by side, then write one causal chain for "what happens when the mutex is taken" that ends in lock convoys.
checklist: a plain Lock has no owner, so re-acquiring it blocks the owner
an RLock keeps owner and count; only the owner can re-enter or release
a free lock is one atomic instruction, no syscall
a taken lock means spin (burn a core) or sleep (pay a wake-up)
hand-off costs ~71× the free lock, so contention, not the lock, is the cost
fix contention by holding less, not by a faster lock

retrieve.q: Explain what "ownership" adds to a mutex, and which Python lock types actually enforce it.
answer: the thread that locked it is the only one allowed to unlock it
a release from any other thread is then an error instead of silently letting a second thread in
RLock (and error-checking pthread mutexes) enforce it; threading.Lock and Semaphore(1) don't

retrieve.q: Walk through what a futex-style mutex does for an uncontended acquire, and then for an acquire while another thread holds it.
answer: uncontended: an atomic instruction in user space flips it to taken; no system call (58 ns acquire + release)
contended: the atomic fails, so the thread asks the kernel to sleep it on that lock
on unlock the holder sees a waiter and asks the kernel to wake one; the waiter must be scheduled again before it runs (microseconds)

retrieve.q: A recursive tree-walk method takes self.lock and calls itself on children. Choose between Lock and RLock, and say what you pay and risk with each.
answer: Lock: the first recursive call self-deadlocks (hangs, or returns False with a timeout)
RLock: works, with small owner/count bookkeeping
risk of RLock: it hides accidental re-entry into a method that assumes the data is consistent; alternatively take the lock once in an outer method and recurse in an unlocked helper

compare.q: A mutex vs a binary semaphore: both let one thread in. What is fundamentally different, which design choice causes it, when would you choose the semaphore anyway, and how does each fail?
answer: the mutex has an owner; a semaphore is a counter anyone may V
no owner is what lets a semaphore be used as a signal: one thread P's, another V's
choose the semaphore for signalling (Semaphore(0) as "done") or counting N permits
the mutex fails by self-deadlock without reentrancy; the semaphore fails silently when a stray V lets two threads in

compare.q: The 4.1 µs hand-off here is half of the thread Event round trip there. What does that number include beyond the mutex itself, and what does it tell you about spinning vs sleeping?
answer: it includes a sleep, a wake-up, a scheduler decision and Python's own work, so it is a ceiling
that is thousands of times a 58 ns free lock
if the holder will release in less than a wake-up's time, spinning briefly is cheaper; otherwise sleep (two-phase)

predict.q: Eight threads each run for _ in range(10**5): with lock: n += 1. The work inside the lock takes nanoseconds. Will 8 threads finish faster than 1 thread doing all 8 × 10⁵ increments? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: No, and possibly much slower. Every increment needs the same lock, so the critical section runs one thread at a time whatever the thread count, and each time the lock passes to a sleeping waiter it costs a wake-up (≈ 4.1 µs, about 71× the 58 ns free lock). One thread pays only uncontended acquires; eight threads can form a convoy. The fix is to hold the lock less: count locally per thread and add once at the end.

apply.task: Using the card's numbers, estimate how many lock hand-offs per second one hot mutex can do if every acquire must wake a sleeping thread (≈ 4.1 µs each), and compare that with the uncontended rate. Then write a recursive depth(node) that takes an RLock at each level on a 3-level tree, and print lock._is_owned() and the recursion level at each acquire and release. Finally, switch it to a plain Lock with acquire(timeout=0.1) and record what happens.
apply.done: You have the two rates (about 244,000 hand-offs/s vs about 17.2 million uncontended/s, roughly 71× apart), a printed RLock trace whose depth goes 1 → 2 → 3 → 2 → 1 → 0, and the plain Lock returning False at depth 2.
apply.hint: 1 / 4.1 µs ≈ 243,900; 1 / 58 ns ≈ 17,241,000. _is_owned() is a private RLock helper; if you'd rather not use it, keep your own depth counter.
